title: i. the boy from pasadena — the room with birds

nodes.text: i. the boy from pasadena — the room with birds

The room at the end is bigger than the others and lit low. One whole wall is a window and through the window is a lake in autumn, flat copper water, reeds gone rust, wild ducks lifting off and settling, lifting off and settling, never all of them up at once.

It takes him a long minute to see the window hangs from the ceiling on a steel arm and the lake is inside it, playing for anybody or nobody. After a while the ducks change and the lake changes, another lake, the same fall.
The voice comes from the bed.
Four of them hold the man down, wrists and shoulders and shins, and he fights them with what he has, which isn't much, and he spends every bit of it. He is trying to get up.
He is trying to get up out of that bed and go someplace and the voice comes out of him angry and desperate and pleading, the words worn off it, only the shape left.
They buckle straps across him. One of them puts a needle in the hose and the fight goes out of him a little at a time.
Two women in the corner, close to him but not around him. The older one has her hand over her mouth. The younger one gets up and goes, fast, right past Jack in the doorway without seeing him at all.

On the floor by the vent where the cold air comes out humming, a big kid is curled up asleep, too big for any bed in the place. He slept through all of it. He sleeps like the hum is a song somebody's singing just to him.

[shot:insert sockets]The man is old, older than any man Jack has ever stood next to. His skin gone yellow like old piano keys and mapped all over with bruises, his gums bleeding, his chest bound up in gauze, his eyes too big for their sockets, rolling around in there and not settling.
Then they settle. They find Jack. They hold on him.

Jack's father was forty-four the night Jack sealed himself into the egg. Dark hair combed wet, a hard jaw, a pipe he never lit, only chewed on while he graded proofs at the kitchen table. Jack has a photograph of him in his billfold gone soft at the corners.
The man in the bed opens his mouth. The voice is quiet now, the anger used up, and it says one word Jack can make out and the word is his name.
Jack knows the voice. He heard it out there in the ruin under the machines and told himself he was only imagining it, and he hears it now and can't tell himself anything.

[shot:insert blanket]He looks at the hand strapped down on the blanket. Square nails. Knuckles knotted up. A little white scar across the back of the thumb from the summer the hatchet slipped up at the lake. Nothing else about the man, only the hand.
Father, Jack says, and it comes out a boy's voice, high and cracked, a kid who stayed out too long after dark.
Jack takes the hand in both of his. It's warm. It grips back, weak, and holds.
Behind him on the hanging glass the ducks lift off the copper water and settle and lift.
